explain.title: Parallel forces
explain.body: Your textbook defines them this way: “All those forces which act parallel to one another are known as parallel forces. The points of application of such forces may be different.” In other words, the forces act along parallel lines, but they do not have to start at the same point.

explain.title: Like parallel forces
explain.body: Your textbook states: “If the parallel forces are acting in the same direction, then they are called like parallel forces”. For example, two parallel upward forces are like parallel forces.

explain.title: Unlike parallel forces
explain.body: Your textbook states: “if their directions are opposite to one another, they are called unlike parallel forces.” For example, an upward force and a downward force along parallel lines are unlike parallel forces.

mistakes: Calling forces like or unlike without first checking that they are parallel.

explain.title: Rigid body and axis of rotation
explain.body: If the distance between two points of the body remains the same under the action of a force, it is called a rigid body. During rotation, the body turns about an axis of rotation.

explain.title: Line of action and moment arm
explain.body: The line along which the force acts is called the line of action of the force. The perpendicular distance of the line of action of a force from the axis of rotation is known as moment arm of the force or simply moment arm.

explain.title: Moment of force or torque
explain.body: Moment of a force or torque is defined as the product of the force and the moment arm. Its magnitude is τ = F×ℓ, and its SI unit is newton metre (N m).

explain.title: Torque direction and couple
explain.body: Torque is positive if the force tends to produce an anticlockwise rotation and negative if it tends to produce a clockwise rotation. When two equal and opposite parallel forces act at two different points of the same body, they form a couple.

explain.title: Resolution of a force
explain.body: To divide a force into its components is known as resolution of a force. The components add together to give the original force.

explain.title: What a component means
explain.body: A component of a vector is its effective value in a given direction. For example, the x-component tells how much of the vector acts along the x-axis.

explain.body: Your textbook defines it this way: “A body is said to be in equilibrium if it has no acceleration.” Forces may act on the body, but they must balance so their resultant is zero.

explain.title: First condition: forces balance
explain.body: By Newton’s second law of motion, F = ma. If a body is in translational equilibrium, then a = 0, therefore, net force F should be 0 or ΣF = 0. A body is said to be in translational equilibrium only if the vector sum of all the external forces acting on it is equal to zero. For coplanar forces, ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0.

explain.title: Second condition: torques balance
explain.body: The second condition of equilibrium implies to the rotational equilibrium which means that the body should not rotate under the action of the forces. The vector sum of all the torques acting on a body about any point must be zero. Mathematically, Στ = 0.

explain.title: Complete equilibrium

explain.title: Equilibrium and support
explain.body: An object is balanced when its centre of mass and its point of support lie on the same vertical line. Then forces on each side are balanced, and the object is said to be in equilibrium.

explain.title: Stable equilibrium
explain.body: A body is said to be in a state of stable equilibrium, if after a slight tilt, it comes back to its original position. A cone on its circular base is stable: tilting raises its centre of gravity, and the resulting torque brings it back.

explain.title: Unstable equilibrium
explain.body: A body is said to be in a state of unstable equilibrium, if after a slight tilt, it tends to move on further away from its original position. A cone balanced on its tip is unstable because tilting makes it fall farther away.

explain.title: Neutral equilibrium
explain.body: A body is in neutral equilibrium, if it comes to rest in its new position after disturbance without any change in its centre of mass. A cylinder rolling on a horizontal surface is an example because the height of its centre of mass remains unchanged.

explain.title: The base of support and toppling
explain.body: A body remains in equilibrium as long as its centre of mass lies within the base. If the line of action of its weight no longer lies inside the base, the body can topple.

mistakes: Do not mix up stable and unstable: stable returns after a slight tilt; unstable moves farther away.
Do not call every object that moves unstable. A rolling cylinder can show neutral equilibrium if its centre of mass stays at the same height.
Do not say a body topples simply because it is tilted; explain whether the line of action of its weight lies outside its base.
Do not confuse the centre of mass with the base of support; both are needed when explaining toppling.

yourTurn.question: How can you prove that the centripetal force always acts perpendicular to velocity?

explain.title: How racing cars are made stable

explain.title: Velocity and force in circular motion

explain.title: Vectors and components
explain.body: A force can be split into two perpendicular rectangular components. For a force F making angle θ with the x-axis, Fx = F cos θ and Fy = F sin θ. Like parallel forces act in the same direction; unlike parallel forces act in opposite directions.

explain.title: Moment and torque
explain.body: The moment of a force is its turning effect about a pivot. It is found by multiplying the force by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to its line of action: τ = rF sin θ. A force acting farther from the pivot has a greater turning effect.

explain.title: Equilibrium
explain.body: A body is in complete equilibrium when the resultant force is zero and the resultant torque is zero: ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0. For a balanced lever, clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments.

explain.title: Centre of gravity and stability
explain.body: A body is more stable when its centre of gravity is lower and its base of support is wider. It topples when the line of action of its weight falls outside its base.

explain.title: Circular motion
explain.body: Centripetal force keeps a body moving in a circular path and is given by Fc = mv²/r. It acts perpendicular to the velocity, changing the velocity's direction.

mistakes: Do not swap the sine and cosine components: for an angle measured from the x-axis, x uses cosine and y uses sine.
Use the perpendicular distance from the pivot when calculating a moment; do not automatically use the full distance if the force is inclined.
Do not confuse the moment arm (a distance) with the moment or torque (a turning effect).
For complete equilibrium, checking only the forces is not enough; the resultant torque must also be zero.
In a moments equation, measure both lever arms from the same pivot and keep units consistent.
Write the correct unit: force is measured in N, distance in m, and torque in N m.
For stability, remember that a high centre of gravity and a narrow base make toppling more likely.

notes.title: Like and Unlike Parallel Forces
notes.answer: Parallel forces act parallel to one another. Same-direction parallel forces are like; opposite-direction parallel forces are unlike.
notes.explanation: Parallel forces act along parallel lines, though they may act at different points. If they point in the same direction, they are like parallel forces; if they point in opposite directions, they are unlike parallel forces.
notes.simple: Check two things: are the forces parallel, and do they point the same way or opposite ways?
examples: Two upward forces acting at different points on a body are like parallel forces.
An upward force and a downward force acting along parallel lines are unlike parallel forces.
steps: Check that the forces act along parallel lines.
If their directions are the same, call them like parallel forces.
If their directions are opposite, call them unlike parallel forces.
notes.checkQuestion: In Fig. 4.1, which pair is unlike parallel forces?
notes.checkAnswer: F₁ and F₂ are like parallel forces; F₂ and F₃ are unlike parallel forces.

notes.title: Adding forces by the head-to-tail rule
notes.answer: The resultant is the single force that has the same effect as the forces acting together.
notes.explanation: A force is a vector, so it has both magnitude and direction. To add forces graphically, draw them head-to-tail. The resultant goes from the tail of the first force to the head of the last force.
notes.simple: Put each force arrowhead-to-tail. The resultant is one arrow from where you started to where you finish.
examples: Forces of 4 N and 3 N placed at right angles have a resultant of 5 N.
In Example 4.1, the measured resultant is 7.1 cm. With the scale 100 N = 1 cm, its magnitude is 710 N.
steps: Choose a suitable scale, such as 100 N = 1 cm.
Draw each force as an arrow using the scale and the given direction.
Place the tail of each new arrow at the head of the previous arrow.
Draw the resultant from the tail of the first arrow to the head of the last arrow.
Measure the resultant and use the scale to find its magnitude; read its direction from the diagram.
notes.checkQuestion: In Example 4.1, what force does a measured resultant length of 7.1 cm represent at the scale 100 N = 1 cm?

notes.title: Torque and the moment arm
notes.answer: Torque is the product of the force and the moment arm: τ = F × ℓ.
notes.explanation: Torque tells us how strongly a force tends to turn an object. It depends on both the size of the force and its moment arm. For example, a door is easier to open when you push at its handle rather than near its hinge. A spanner turns a nut more easily when you apply force farther from the nut.
notes.simple: Torque is the turning effect of a force. A bigger force or a longer moment arm gives a greater turning effect.
examples: A door handle is placed far from the hinge so a smaller force can turn the door.
A force of 400 N applied at the end of a 0.25 m spanner produces a torque of 100 N m.
steps: Identify the force and its perpendicular distance from the axis.
Use τ = F × ℓ.
Multiply the force by the moment arm.
Give the torque in newton metres (N m).
notes.checkQuestion: A force of 20 N acts perpendicularly at a moment arm of 0.4 m. What is the moment arm?

notes.title: Resolving a Force into Components
notes.answer: The x-component is found using cosine, and the y-component is found using sine.
notes.explanation: A force can be split into perpendicular x- and y-components. If the force F makes an angle θ with the x-axis, use cosine for the x-component and sine for the y-component.
notes.simple: Think of the force as the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle. Its horizontal part uses cosine, and its vertical part uses sine.
examples: For F = 200 N at 30° to the x-axis: F_x = 200 cos 30° = 173.2 N.
For the same force: F_y = 200 sin 30° = 100 N.
steps: Identify F and the angle θ it makes with the x-axis.
Use F_x = F cos θ.
Use F_y = F sin θ.
Substitute the values and calculate each component.
notes.checkQuestion: A force of 10 N makes an angle of 30° with the x-axis. What are its x- and y-components?
notes.checkAnswer: F_x = F cos θ; F_y = F sin θ. For 200 N at 30°: F_x = 173.2 N and F_y = 100 N.

notes.title: Finding a Force from Its Perpendicular Components
notes.explanation: A force can be split into two perpendicular components: one along the x-axis and one along the y-axis. If these components are known, use Pythagoras to find the force’s magnitude and the tangent ratio to find its direction.
notes.simple: The x- and y-components are the horizontal and vertical parts of a force. Join them at a right angle: Pythagoras gives the force’s size, and tan⁻¹ gives its angle.
examples: If F_x = 3 N and F_y = 4 N, then F = √(3² + 4²) = 5 N.
For the same components, θ = tan⁻¹(4/3) ≈ 53.1°.
steps: Use F = √(F_x² + F_y²) to find the magnitude.
Use θ = tan⁻¹(F_y/F_x) to find the direction.
State the magnitude in newtons and the angle with its reference direction.
notes.checkQuestion: If F_x = 3 N and F_y = 4 N, what are the magnitude and direction of the force measured from the positive x-axis?

notes.title: Principle of Moments
notes.answer: When a body is in balanced position, the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about that point.
notes.explanation: A body is balanced when the total clockwise moment about a point equals the total anticlockwise moment about that point. A moment is calculated by multiplying the force by its perpendicular distance from the pivot.
notes.simple: Think of a seesaw: a smaller force can balance a larger one if it acts farther from the pivot.
examples: A 10 N force acting 0.2 m from a pivot makes a moment of 10 × 0.2 = 2 N m.
If a 30 N force acts 0.4 m from a pivot, its moment is 30 × 0.4 = 12 N m.
steps: Choose the pivot or point about which the body turns.
Work out each moment using force × perpendicular distance from the pivot.
Separate the moments that turn clockwise from those that turn anticlockwise.
For balance, set total clockwise moments equal to total anticlockwise moments.
Solve the equation and include the correct unit.
notes.checkQuestion: What must be equal for a body to balance about a point?
notes.checkAnswer: The clockwise and anticlockwise moments are equal.

notes.title: Centre of Gravity and Centre of Mass
notes.answer: For an irregular plane lamina, the centre of gravity is at the intersection of the vertical lines drawn when the lamina is suspended from different points.
notes.explanation: An object's weight acts as if it is concentrated at one point called its centre of gravity. Its mass can also be treated as concentrated at one point called its centre of mass. In a uniform gravitational field, these points coincide. For an irregular plane lamina, suspend it from two different points and draw the vertical line each time; their intersection gives its centre of gravity.
notes.simple: Think of the centre of gravity as the point where an object's weight seems to act. For an irregular flat shape, hang it from two places: the crossing of the two vertical lines shows that point.
examples: A rectangle's centre of gravity is at the intersection of its diagonals.
A cup's centre of gravity can lie outside the material of the cup.
steps: Make a small hole near the edge of the lamina and suspend it freely from that point.
Hang a plumb line from the same point of suspension.
When the lamina stops moving, draw the vertical line along the plumb line.
Suspend the lamina from a different point and draw a second vertical line.
Mark the point where the two lines cross; this is the centre of gravity.
notes.checkQuestion: When an irregular plane lamina is suspended from two different points, where is its centre of gravity?
notes.checkAnswer: The point where the two vertical lines cross.

notes.title: Equilibrium: balanced forces, no acceleration
notes.answer: A body is in equilibrium if it has no acceleration. It can be at rest in static equilibrium or move with uniform velocity in dynamic equilibrium.
notes.explanation: A body is in equilibrium when it has no acceleration. It may be at rest (static equilibrium) or move with uniform velocity (dynamic equilibrium). Forces balance when their resultant is zero.
notes.simple: Equilibrium means there is no change in the body's motion: it stays at rest or keeps moving at the same velocity.
examples: A book resting on a table is in static equilibrium: the table’s upward normal force balances the book’s downward weight.
A paratrooper descending with uniform velocity is in dynamic equilibrium: air resistance balances gravity.
steps: Check whether the body has acceleration.
If it has no acceleration, it is in equilibrium.
If it is at rest, it is in static equilibrium.
If it moves with uniform velocity, it is in dynamic equilibrium.
Forces acting on it balance when their resultant is zero.
notes.checkQuestion: What type of equilibrium describes a body moving with uniform velocity?
notes.checkAnswer: A body moving with uniform velocity is in dynamic equilibrium.

notes.title: Conditions of Equilibrium
notes.explanation: For complete equilibrium, the forces must balance in both directions and the turning effects must balance too. This means the object has no acceleration and no rotation.
notes.simple: An object is completely in equilibrium when it neither speeds up or slows down nor starts turning.
examples: A picture hanging still has balanced upward tensions and downward weight.
Two equal and opposite forces along different lines can have zero resultant force but still turn a body.
steps: Choose the object you are studying and show the forces acting on it.
Choose x- and y-axes that make resolving forces as easy as possible.
Resolve forces into components if needed.
Use ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0.
If needed, use Στ = 0 and solve the equations.
notes.checkQuestion: What three sums must be zero for a body to be in complete equilibrium?
notes.checkAnswer: The vector sum of all external forces is zero, and the vector sum of all torques about any point is zero.

notes.title: States of Equilibrium
notes.answer: The three states are stable, unstable and neutral equilibrium.
notes.explanation: A body's equilibrium state depends on what happens when it is tilted or disturbed. A stable body returns to its starting position; an unstable body moves farther away; a neutral body rests in its new position. The centre of mass and the base of support help explain whether a body topples.
notes.simple: Ask what the body does after a small push: return means stable, move farther away means unstable, and stay in its new position means neutral.
examples: A cone standing on its circular base is stable: a slight tilt raises its centre of gravity, and the resulting torque brings it back.
A cylinder rolling on a flat surface is neutral: its centre of mass stays at the same height as it moves.
steps: Imagine the body has been disturbed slightly.
Check whether it returns, moves farther away, or stays in its new position.
Use the body's centre of mass and base of support to explain why.
notes.checkQuestion: What state of equilibrium does a cone standing on its circular base show?
notes.checkAnswer: A cone on its circular base is in stable equilibrium.

notes.title: Improving stability
notes.answer: Improve stability by lowering the centre of gravity or widening the base.
notes.explanation: Stability depends on where an object's centre of gravity is and how wide its base is. A low centre of gravity and a wide base make toppling less likely.
notes.simple: An object is harder to tip over when its weight is low down or spread over a wider base.
examples: A low armchair is more stable than a high chair because its centre of gravity is lower.
A bus carrying heavy loads on its floor has a lower centre of gravity than one carrying those loads on its roof.
steps: Put heavy parts or loads as low as possible.
Make the base wider if the design allows.
If an object tilts, consider whether its weight and the ground's reaction form a turning couple that will topple it.
notes.checkQuestion: How can you improve the stability of an object?
notes.checkAnswer: Lower its centre of gravity or widen its base.

notes.title: Stability and motion in a circle
notes.answer: A racing car is made more stable by keeping its centre of mass low and increasing its base area. A balancing toy returns to its stable position by lowering its centre of gravity. A body moving in a circle has velocity along the tangent and needs a force perpendicular to its velocity to keep moving in the circle.
notes.explanation: Racing cars and balancing toys are designed using ideas about stability. A low centre of mass and a wide base help a car resist toppling. In a balancing toy, the centre of gravity is below the pivot, so disturbing the toy raises its centre of gravity; it returns to its stable position by lowering it. In circular motion, the velocity points along the tangent, while the force needed to keep the body moving in a circle acts perpendicular to the velocity.
notes.simple: A low, wide object is harder to tip over. A balancing toy returns to its resting position by lowering its centre of gravity. In circular motion, the force points inward and the velocity points along the circle’s tangent.
examples: A racing car is made more stable by keeping its centre of mass low and its wheels outside the main body, which increases its base area.
A balancing toy returns to its original position after it is disturbed because it lowers its centre of gravity.
steps: Keep the centre of mass as low as possible.
Increase the base area, for example by keeping the wheels outside the main body.
For a balancing toy, identify the pivot and check that its centre of gravity is below it.
For circular motion, draw the velocity along the tangent and the force towards the centre; these directions are perpendicular.
notes.checkQuestion: What two design features improve the stability of a racing car?
notes.checkAnswer: A low centre of mass and a wide base area.

notes.title: Centripetal Force
notes.answer: Centripetal force is the force that keeps an object moving in a circle at constant speed. It acts towards the centre and is perpendicular to the object's velocity.
notes.explanation: Centripetal force keeps an object moving in a circular path at constant speed. Its direction is towards the centre of the circle, while the object's velocity is along the tangent. For example, tension in a string keeps a whirled stone moving in a circle, and Earth's gravity keeps a satellite in orbit.
notes.simple: Centripetal force is the inward pull that keeps an object going around a circle instead of flying off in a straight line.
examples: A string provides the centripetal force for a stone being whirled in a circle.
Earth's gravitational pull provides the centripetal force for a satellite orbiting Earth.
steps: Write the relation: F_c = mv²/r.
Convert mass to kilograms and identify the speed and radius.
Substitute the values into the relation.
Calculate the force and write its unit, newtons (N).
notes.checkQuestion: In circular motion, which way does centripetal force act compared with the object's velocity?
notes.checkAnswer: The force acts towards the centre; the velocity is along the tangent, so they are perpendicular.

notes.title: Turning Effects of Force
notes.answer: Complete equilibrium requires zero resultant force and zero resultant torque.
notes.explanation: For a force to turn a body, its turning effect (torque) depends on the force and its perpendicular distance from the pivot. A body is in complete equilibrium when both the resultant force and the resultant torque are zero.
notes.simple: A force can push or pull an object, and it can also make the object turn. How strongly it turns depends on how big the force is and how far from the pivot it acts.
examples: A 10 N force acting 0.5 m from a pivot at right angles produces torque 10 × 0.5 = 5 N m.
A 200 N force at 30° to the horizontal has components Fx = 200 cos 30° = 173.2 N and Fy = 200 sin 30° = 100 N.
steps: Resolve a force into components using Fx = F cos θ and Fy = F sin θ when θ is measured from the x-axis.
For torque, use τ = rF sin θ, where r is the distance from the pivot to the point of application of force.
For a balanced body, clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments.
For complete equilibrium, ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0.
For circular motion, centripetal force is Fc = mv²/r and acts perpendicular to the velocity.
notes.checkQuestion: What two conditions must be satisfied for complete equilibrium?
notes.checkAnswer: Both the resultant force and the resultant torque must be zero.

quiz.stem: A body has ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0, but Στ is not zero. What is true?

A non-zero sum of torques means rotational equilibrium is not satisfied.

quiz.stem: A picture hangs at rest from two strings. Which statement describes its equilibrium?
options: The centre of gravity is at the highest position
The upward forces equal the downward forces and the torque sum is zero
Every force on the body is zero
rationales: This is not a condition for equilibrium.
At rest, its forces and torques balance; these are the equilibrium conditions.
Individual forces can be non-zero while their vector sum is zero.

quiz.stem: What happens to a body in stable equilibrium after a slight tilt?
options: It returns to its original position
It moves farther away from its original position
It stays in its new position
rationales: This is the defining behaviour of stable equilibrium.
Moving farther away describes unstable equilibrium.
Remaining in the new position describes neutral equilibrium.
Stable equilibrium does not mean that the body must topple.

quiz.stem: What happens to the centre of mass when a cone standing on its base is tilted slightly?
options: Its centre of mass is lowered on tilting
Its centre of mass is raised on tilting
Its centre of mass stays at the same height

Tilting a cone on its base raises its centre of mass, helping produce a restoring effect.
Unchanged height is associated with neutral equilibrium.

quiz.stem: A cone balanced on its tip falls farther away from its original position after a slight tilt. What state is this?
rationales: A stable body would return to its starting position.
Moving farther away after a slight tilt is unstable equilibrium.
A neutral body would rest in its new position without moving farther away.

quiz.stem: Why does a cylinder rolling on a horizontal surface show neutral equilibrium?
options: Its centre of mass remains at the same height
Its centre of mass rises continuously
Its centre of mass falls continuously
rationales: The height of the cylinder's centre of mass remains unchanged as it rolls.
A continuous rise in centre-of-mass height is not the reason for neutral equilibrium.
A continuous fall would cause the body to move farther away, not describe the stated neutral case.

quiz.stem: Why can a body topple when its centre of mass is no longer above its base of support?
options: The weight's line of action lies outside the base of support
The floor stops exerting a reaction
rationales: The body topples when the line of action of its weight no longer lies within the base of support.
Toppling does not require the body's weight to become larger.
The floor can still exert a reaction while the body topples.
The centre of mass does not disappear when the body is tilted.

quiz.stem: Which object is an example of stable equilibrium?
options: A ball resting on a horizontal surface
A cone standing on its circular base
A cone balanced on its tip
A body that returns after a slight tilt

A cone on its circular base returns after a slight tilt and is stable.
A cone balanced on its tip is unstable.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes neutral equilibrium?
options: The height of its centre of mass changes
It comes to rest in its new position without a change in its centre of mass
It always returns to its original position
It moves farther away from its original position
rationales: A change in centre-of-mass height is not the defining feature of neutral equilibrium.
This gives the defining behaviour of neutral equilibrium.
Returning to the original position describes stable equilibrium.
Moving farther away describes unstable equilibrium.

quiz.stem: For a balanced body to remain supported without toppling, which condition is important?
options: The body's centre of mass is always outside its body
The body's centre of mass lies above the base of support
The body has no point of support

The weight acts downward, not horizontally.
A balanced supported body has a point of support.

quiz.stem: Which change generally makes a standing object more stable?
options: Place all its load at the top.
rationales: Raising the centre of gravity generally makes toppling easier, not harder.
A lower centre of gravity makes the object more stable.
A narrower base generally makes the object less stable.

quiz.stem: Why does placing heavy loads on the floor of a bus improve its stability?
options: It lowers the bus's centre of gravity.
It raises the bus's centre of gravity.
It makes the bus's base narrower.
rationales: Loads low down lower the bus's centre of gravity, improving stability.
Loads on the floor do not raise the centre of gravity; they lower it.
Placing loads on the floor does not make the bus's base narrower.

quiz.stem: Which design change can improve the stability of a system?
options: Place its heaviest parts as high as possible.
rationales: A wider base makes toppling less likely.
A higher centre of gravity makes toppling more likely.
A narrower base generally reduces stability.
Putting heavy parts high raises the centre of gravity and reduces stability.

quiz.stem: Which combination is most helpful for improving stability?
options: A low centre of gravity and a wide base.
A high centre of gravity and a narrow base.
A high centre of gravity and a wide base only.
A low centre of gravity and a narrow base only.
rationales: Both a low centre of gravity and a wide base improve stability.
Both a high centre of gravity and a narrow base tend to reduce stability.
A high centre of gravity is not helpful for stability.
A narrow base is not helpful for stability.

quiz.stem: A bus loaded with heavy steel sheets on its top is less stable mainly because:
options: Its centre of gravity is raised.
Its centre of gravity is lowered.
rationales: Putting heavy loads high raises the bus's centre of gravity.
The centre of gravity is raised, not lowered.
The loading described does not make the base wider.
The bus's weight does not disappear when it is loaded.

quiz.stem: In the tilted-chair illustration, what does the couple formed by the chair's weight and the ground's reaction tend to do?
options: It forms a clockwise couple that tends to overturn the chair backward.
It lowers the chair's centre of gravity and restores it upright.
It makes the chair's base wider.
It removes the reaction force from the ground.

The described couple tends to overturn the chair, not restore it upright.
Tilting the chair does not make its base wider.
The ground's reaction force is shown; it is not removed.

quiz.stem: A body in stable equilibrium is generally in a position where its centre of gravity is:
options: It is stable because its centre of gravity is at its lowest position.
It is unstable because its centre of gravity is at its lowest position.
It is stable only if it has a narrow base.
It cannot be affected by a turning couple.
rationales: A stable position corresponds to a low position of the centre of gravity.
A low centre of gravity is associated with stability, not instability.
A narrow base generally does not improve stability.
A turning couple can affect a body, so it is not immune to one.

quiz.stem: Which loading and design choice would best help a double-decker bus resist overturning?
options: Loads low down and a broad base.
Loads high up and a broad base.
Loads low down and a narrow base.
Loads high up and a narrow base.
rationales: Low loads lower the centre of gravity, and a broad base improves stability.
A broad base helps, but high loads raise the centre of gravity.
Low loads help, but a narrow base is less stable.
Both high loads and a narrow base tend to reduce stability.

quiz.stem: Which design change best improves the stability of a racing car?
options: Keep the centre of mass high and make the base narrow.
Keep the centre of mass low and increase the base area.
Keep the centre of mass low and make the base narrow.
Keep the centre of mass high and increase the base area.
rationales: A high centre of mass and narrow base make toppling easier.
Correct: a low centre of mass and a wider base make toppling less likely.
A narrow base reduces stability even if the centre of mass is low.
A high centre of mass makes toppling more likely despite the wider base.

quiz.stem: Where does the centre of gravity of a balancing toy remain in its stable state?
options: At the edge of the toy.
At any position, because its position does not matter.
rationales: A centre of gravity above the pivot would not describe the stable arrangement given in the section.
Correct: in these toys the centre of gravity remains below the pivot point.
The section does not say that it remains at the edge of the toy.
The position matters; the section states that it remains below the pivot.

quiz.stem: What happens to a balancing toy when it is disturbed from its stable position?
options: It becomes lower, so the toy moves farther from its initial position.
It is raised, and the toy returns by lowering it.
It stays at the same height, so the toy remains disturbed.
It moves above the pivot and stays there.
rationales: The section says the centre of gravity is raised when the toy is disturbed.
Correct: it is raised momentarily, then lowered as the toy returns to its stable position.
The centre of gravity is raised when the toy is disturbed, not kept at the same height.
The section says the centre of gravity is below the pivot in the stable state; it does not say the toy stays above the pivot.

quiz.stem: Which rotational-motion quantity plays the same role as force does in translational motion?

Angular acceleration is paired with acceleration, not force.

Angular momentum is paired with momentum, not force.

quiz.stem: In which direction is the velocity of a body moving along a circular path at any point?

Along the tangent to the circular path.
Towards the centre of the circle.
At right angles to the plane of the circle.

quiz.stem: For uniform-speed motion in a circular path, how is the required force directed relative to velocity?

It has no relation to velocity.

quiz.stem: Why must the force in uniform circular motion be perpendicular to the velocity?
options: It would have a component along the velocity and change the magnitude of velocity.
It would make the centre of gravity lower.
It would increase the base area of the object.
It would change the tangent into a radius.

The direction of force cannot change the object's base area.

quiz.stem: In uniform circular motion, what is the direction of centripetal force?
options: Towards the centre of the circle
Along the tangent to the circle
Away from the centre of the circle
In the direction of the object's velocity
rationales: This is correct: centripetal force is always directed towards the centre.
The tangent gives the direction of velocity, not centripetal force.
Centripetal force points inward, not away from the centre.
Velocity is along the tangent and is perpendicular to centripetal force.

quiz.stem: Which relation gives the magnitude of centripetal force?
rationales: This is correct: the textbook relation is F_c = mv²/r.

quiz.stem: At any point on a circular path, in which direction does the object's velocity act?
options: The velocity is along the radius
The velocity is along the tangent to the circle
The velocity points towards the centre
The velocity points away from the centre
rationales: The radius points towards the centre and is not the direction of velocity.
This is correct: velocity acts along the tangent to the circular path.
This describes the direction of centripetal force, not velocity.
Velocity is tangent to the path, not directed away from its centre.

quiz.stem: What provides the centripetal force when a stone is whirled in a circle on a string?
rationales: This is correct: tension in the string pulls the stone towards the centre.
The textbook example identifies string tension as the centripetal force; gravity is neglected there.
Speed is a property of the motion, not the force supplying the inward pull.
The tangent indicates the velocity direction and does not provide the inward force.

quiz.stem: What supplies the centripetal force that keeps the Moon in orbit around Earth?
options: The Moon's distance from Earth alone
The Moon's velocity along its orbit
rationales: Speed alone does not provide the force needed to keep the Moon in its orbit.
This is correct: Earth's gravitational pull supplies the necessary centripetal force.
Distance alone is not a force and cannot supply centripetal force.
Velocity describes the Moon's motion; Earth's gravity supplies the inward force.

quiz.stem: In a rapidly rotating washing-machine dryer, what provides centripetal force to the clothes?
options: Friction between the clothes and drum wall
rationales: This is correct: friction between the clothes and drum walls provides the needed centripetal force.
The textbook explanation identifies friction with the drum wall, not weight, as the source.
The holes let water escape but do not provide the clothes' centripetal force.
The textbook explanation does not identify the air as the source of the centripetal force.

quiz.stem: For an object of fixed mass moving in a circle of fixed radius, what happens to centripetal force if its speed increases?
options: Increasing the radius increases centripetal force
Increasing the speed increases centripetal force
Centripetal force is independent of mass
Centripetal force is always zero at constant speed
rationales: At fixed mass and speed, a greater radius gives a smaller force because F_c = mv²/r.
This is correct: centripetal force is proportional to the square of speed.
The relation includes mass, so centripetal force depends on mass.
A constant speed in a circular path still requires centripetal force to change the direction of motion.

quiz.stem: Why can water escape through the holes of a rapidly rotating dryer drum?
options: The water molecules receive a larger centripetal force than the clothes
The water molecules cannot get the required centripetal force to move in circular paths
The drum stops rotating when the water reaches the holes
The water molecules move towards the centre of the drum

The drum continues rotating; its rotation is what helps separate water from the clothes.

quiz.stem: Q4.7. In stable equilibrium, the centre of gravity of the body lies:
rationales: A high centre of gravity does not describe stable equilibrium.

quiz.stem: Q4.8. The centre of mass of a body:

may lie within , outside or on the surface
rationales: The centre of mass can be outside the material of a shaped body, such as a ring.

quiz.stem: Q4.9. A cylinder resting on its circular base is in:
rationales: This is correct because a small displacement raises its centre of gravity and it tends to return to its original position.
